exercises.title: Products over £100
exercises.prompt: Using the Products table, list the name, category and unit price of every product with a unit price above 100, most expensive first.
hints: Filter with WHERE. Numbers are written without quotes.
Sort with ORDER BY ... DESC.
exercises.model_query: SELECT ProductName, Category, UnitPrice FROM Products WHERE UnitPrice > 100 ORDER BY UnitPrice DESC;

exercises.title: Biggest campaigns
exercises.prompt: Using the Campaigns table, list the name, channel and spend of the 3 campaigns with the highest spend, highest first.
hints: Sort the campaigns by CampaignSpend.
ORDER BY CampaignSpend DESC puts the highest spend at the top.
LIMIT keeps only the first rows of a sorted result. It goes at the very end of the query.
exercises.model_query: SELECT CampaignName, Channel, CampaignSpend FROM Campaigns ORDER BY CampaignSpend DESC LIMIT 3;

exercises.title: Mobile app orders in March
exercises.prompt: Using the Orders table, list the OrderID, CustomerID and OrderDate of every order placed in March 2025 through the 'Mobile App' sales channel, earliest first.
hints: You need two conditions at the same time, one on SalesChannel and one on OrderDate. Join them with AND.
Text values go in single quotes and must match exactly, capital letters and spaces included: 'Mobile App'.
Dates are stored as text like 2025-03-15, so they compare correctly. OrderDate BETWEEN '2025-03-01' AND '2025-03-31' keeps the whole of March, both ends included. Finish with ORDER BY OrderDate.
exercises.model_query: SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate FROM Orders WHERE SalesChannel = 'Mobile App' AND OrderDate BETWEEN '2025-03-01' AND '2025-03-31' ORDER BY OrderDate;

exercises.title: Campaigns per channel
exercises.prompt: Using the Campaigns table, show one row for each marketing channel with the number of campaigns that used it and their average spend, rounded to 2 decimal places. Use the exact column names Channel, CampaignCount and AverageSpend.
hints: Group the campaigns by channel with GROUP BY Channel.
COUNT(*) counts the rows in each group and AVG(CampaignSpend) averages their spend. ROUND(x, 2) rounds x to 2 decimal places.
Rename a column with AS, for example COUNT(*) AS CampaignCount. This exercise checks your column names.
exercises.model_query: SELECT Channel, COUNT(*) AS CampaignCount, ROUND(AVG(CampaignSpend), 2) AS AverageSpend FROM Campaigns GROUP BY Channel;

exercises.title: Orders with no campaign
exercises.prompt: Some orders did not come from a marketing campaign, so their CampaignID is empty (NULL). Using the Orders table, count these orders for each sales channel. Show two columns: SalesChannel, then the number of orders with no campaign.
hints: An empty value is called NULL. Nothing is ever equal to NULL, so CampaignID = NULL matches no rows at all.
Test for an empty value with IS NULL. Do this in WHERE, so that only the orders with no campaign are left.
WHERE runs before the rows are grouped. After it, GROUP BY SalesChannel and count the rows in each group with COUNT(*). COUNT(CampaignID) would give 0 here, because counting a column skips the NULLs.
exercises.model_query: SELECT SalesChannel, COUNT(*) AS OrderCount FROM Orders WHERE CampaignID IS NULL GROUP BY SalesChannel;

exercises.title: Best-selling products
exercises.prompt: Using the OrderItems table, add up the Quantity of each product across all of its order lines, and find every product with a total of at least 40 units. Show two columns: ProductID, then the total number of units.
hints: Each row of OrderItems is one line of an order, and Quantity is the number of units on that line. Add the quantities up for each product with GROUP BY ProductID and SUM(Quantity).
WHERE filters individual rows before they are grouped, so it cannot test a total. To filter on a total, use HAVING.
HAVING goes after GROUP BY and can use an aggregate, for example HAVING SUM(Quantity) compared with 40.
exercises.model_query: SELECT ProductID, SUM(Quantity) AS UnitsSold FROM OrderItems GROUP BY ProductID HAVING SUM(Quantity) >= 40;

exercises.title: Revenue by region
exercises.prompt: Using the Customers, Orders and OrderItems tables, work out the revenue for each customer region from orders whose OrderStatus is 'Completed'. The revenue of a line is Quantity * UnitPriceAtSale * (1 - DiscountRate). Add the lines up for each region, then round that total to 2 decimal places. Show two columns: Region, then revenue. Put the region with the highest revenue first.
hints: Region is in Customers, OrderStatus is in Orders, and the quantity, price and discount are in OrderItems. You need all three tables.
Join Customers to Orders on CustomerID, then Orders to OrderItems on OrderID. Filter with WHERE before you GROUP BY Region.
Do the multiplication inside SUM(...), and put ROUND(..., 2) around the whole SUM. Sort by the revenue column with DESC.
exercises.model_query: SELECT c.Region, ROUND(SUM(oi.Quantity * oi.UnitPriceAtSale * (1 - oi.DiscountRate)), 2) AS Revenue FROM Customers c JOIN Orders o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID JOIN OrderItems oi ON oi.OrderID = o.OrderID WHERE o.OrderStatus = 'Completed' GROUP BY c.Region ORDER BY Revenue DESC;

exercises.title: Customers with no orders
exercises.prompt: Find every customer who has never placed an order. Show CustomerID and CustomerName.
hints: You need Customers on one side and Orders on the other, and the customers you want are the ones with no match in Orders.
An INNER JOIN drops customers with no orders. A LEFT JOIN from Customers keeps them, and fills the Orders columns with NULL.
After the LEFT JOIN, keep only the rows where OrderID IS NULL. Do not test CampaignID: a real order can have an empty CampaignID too.
exercises.model_query: SELECT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName FROM Customers c LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID WHERE o.OrderID IS NULL;

exercises.title: Orders and customers by month
exercises.prompt: Using the Orders table, show one row for each month that has orders. Use three columns: Month (the text YYYY-MM, for example 2025-03), OrderCount (the number of orders placed in that month) and CustomerCount (the number of different customers who placed them). Put the earliest month first.
hints: OrderDate is text such as 2025-03-15. strftime('%Y-%m', OrderDate) turns it into a month label such as 2025-03.

GROUP BY that month label. COUNT(*) counts the orders in a month. A customer can order more than once in a month, so COUNT(CustomerID) would count some customers twice. COUNT(DISTINCT ...) counts different customers.
Name the three columns with AS, and finish with ORDER BY on the month. GROUP BY does not promise any order, so the ORDER BY is what guarantees the earliest month comes first.
exercises.model_query: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', OrderDate) AS Month, COUNT(*) AS OrderCount, COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) AS CustomerCount FROM Orders GROUP BY Month ORDER BY Month;

exercises.title: Running total of orders
exercises.prompt: Show how the number of orders builds up through the year. Use one row for each month and three columns in this order: the month as the text YYYY-MM, the number of orders placed in that month, and the running total, meaning the number of orders placed from the start of the year up to and including that month. Put the earliest month first.
hints: Start with the query that gives one row per month with its number of orders, as in the previous exercise. Put it in a CTE, a WITH name AS (...) block placed before the main SELECT.
Then SELECT from the CTE and add a window function: SUM(...) OVER (...) adds values up across rows without collapsing the rows.
Inside OVER, an ORDER BY on the month makes the sum run from the first month up to the current row. The last month should show 200, the number of orders in the table.
exercises.model_query: WITH MonthlyOrders AS (SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', OrderDate) AS Month, COUNT(*) AS OrderCount FROM Orders GROUP BY Month) SELECT Month, OrderCount, SUM(OrderCount) OVER (ORDER BY Month) AS RunningTotal FROM MonthlyOrders ORDER BY Month;

exercises.title: Customer value bands
exercises.prompt: Put each customer into a value band by how much they spent on orders whose OrderStatus is 'Completed'. The value of a line is Quantity * UnitPriceAtSale * (1 - DiscountRate), and a customer's spend is the sum of the lines on their Completed orders. The bands are 'High value' for a spend of 5000 or more, 'Mid value' for 2000 or more but less than 5000, and 'Low value' for less than 2000. Leave out customers who have no Completed orders. Show one row for each band with two columns: the band name, then the number of customers in that band. Use the band names exactly as written here.
hints: First get one row per customer with their spend. Join Orders to OrderItems on OrderID, keep the Completed orders with WHERE, and GROUP BY CustomerID. Put this step in a CTE or a subquery.
That join only returns customers who have a Completed order, so the others are left out already. You do not need the Customers table.

Turn each spend into a band name with CASE WHEN ... THEN '...' ... END. CASE stops at the first condition that is true, so test the highest band first. Then GROUP BY the band and count the customers in each.
exercises.model_query: WITH CustomerSpend AS (SELECT o.CustomerID, SUM(oi.Quantity * oi.UnitPriceAtSale * (1 - oi.DiscountRate)) AS Spend FROM Orders o JOIN OrderItems oi ON oi.OrderID = o.OrderID WHERE o.OrderStatus = 'Completed' GROUP BY o.CustomerID) SELECT CASE WHEN Spend >= 5000 THEN 'High value' WHEN Spend >= 2000 THEN 'Mid value' ELSE 'Low value' END AS ValueBand, COUNT(*) AS CustomerCount FROM CustomerSpend GROUP BY ValueBand;
